title: Observation of the orbital Nernst effect
authors: Yuto Masuda, Takamasa Hirai, Daegeun Jo, Naoki Yano, Peter M. Oppeneer, Hossein Sepehri-Amin, Ken-ichi Uchida, Kazuya Ando
abstract: The Nernst effect, which converts a temperature gradient into a transverse charge current, is fundamental to thermoelectrics. Its spin analogue, the spin Nernst effect, enables thermal generation of transverse spin currents and is central to spin caloritronics. Recently, the discovery of orbital currents, the orbital counterpart of spin currents, has extended angular-momentum transport beyond spin, leading to the prediction of the orbital Nernst effect, in which a temperature gradient drives a transverse orbital current. However, experimental evidence for this effect has been lacking. Here, we report the observation of the orbital Nernst effect in Ti. Using Ni electrodes on Ti, we detect a thermally induced voltage that depends on the magnetization direction and scales linearly with the temperature gradient. This voltage is strongly suppressed both when Ni is replaced with Ni$_{81}$Fe$_{19}$ and when Ti is replaced with Cr, providing strong evidence that the signal originates from the orbital Nernst effect rather than the anomalous Nernst or spin Nernst effect. These results establish thermally driven orbital transport, opening a pathway toward orbital caloritronics.
summary: This work reports the first experimental observation of the orbital Nernst effect in a solid-state device using Ti/Ni junctions. By generating a temperature gradient via Joule heating and measuring the resulting transverse voltage, the authors provide strong evidence for thermally driven orbital transport. This opens a new field, orbital caloritronics, by demonstrating a mechanism beyond traditional spin or charge transport.
main_problem: The primary goal was the experimental observation and confirmation of the orbital Nernst effect, which predicts a transverse orbital current driven by a temperature gradient.
main_result: The authors successfully detected a measurable, magnetization-dependent voltage signal in Ti/Ni devices that scales linearly with the temperature gradient, strongly suggesting the orbital Nernst effect.
method:
The experiment involved applying a DC current to generate a controlled Joule heating-induced temperature gradient ($
abla T$) across a Ti cross-bar, and measuring the resulting transverse voltage using Ni electrodes.
model_or_system: The physical system is a metal/ferromagnet junction (e.g., Ti/Ni or Cr/Ni). The measurement relies on the orbital-to-spin conversion occurring at the interface, allowing the detection of orbital currents via spin accumulation.

figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup using thermography to map temperature gradients, showing the measured voltage ($\Delta V$) dependence on magnetic field and heating current, and comparing results between Ti and Cr samples.
paper_structure:
The paper establishes the theoretical background of orbital transport, details the experimental setup using high-resolution thermography to generate $
abla T$, presents the measurements showing the $\Delta V$ dependence on $
abla T$ and magnetization, and concludes by using material substitutions to confirm the orbital nature of the effect.
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter/thermoelectrics, the study of orbital currents and their coupling to thermal gradients touches upon non-equilibrium transport phenomena that are relevant to understanding energy dissipation and thermalization in quantum systems.
